LESSON 57 OF 106·Data Protection and Endpoint Security

Ransomware: Encryption, Double Extortion and Recovery

How ransomware actually denies you your data, why modern operators steal before they encrypt, and which decisions made long before the ransom note decide the outcome.

Foundation15 min
Why this matters

Modern ransomware usually does two things: it encrypts the data and it copies it first. The copy is what creates pressure, because the victim can restore but cannot be sure the data was not taken.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Initial access is followed by a period of quiet activity while the attacker prepares, which is the most useful detection window.
  • Data is often exfiltrated before encryption, so the theft is complete even if every system is restored.
  • Encryption then disrupts operations, usually in batches so recovery is deliberately painful.
  • Backups that share credentials or network access with production are often reached by the same attacker.
  • Recovery is a business decision under pressure, which is exactly when paying becomes tempting.

The background

  • Early ransomware encrypted one machine at a time and was largely a nuisance.
  • Crypto-ransomware made payment meaningful, and criminal groups built around it.
  • Exfiltration before encryption introduced the double-extortion model and changed the negotiation position.
  • Ransomware-as-a-service lowered the skill barrier, and affiliate models scaled it.

Real-world examples

  • An organisation that restores quickly still has to act on the assumption that data was taken.
  • Backups reachable with the same domain administrator account as production are effectively inside the blast radius.
  • A network share used for file access can be encrypted far faster than a server, and it is where business data usually lives.

What to look for

  • Check whether backups are isolated from production in both credentials and network path.
  • Check whether the backup catalogue itself is protected, since deleting backups defeats everything.
  • Check how long a full restore would actually take, measured rather than assumed.
  • Check whether the decision-making path for a ransomware incident is written down and known.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

CISA #StopRansomware Guide worked through as a recovery rehearsal

Reading CISA's joint ransomware guidance and turning its prevention and response sections into a personal checklist, naming which copy you would restore and what would stop you

Open CISA resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Keep backups immutable or offline, so encryption cannot reach them.
  • Use separate credentials for backup administration, so one compromise does not do both.
  • Test full restores on a schedule and record the real elapsed time.
  • Segment aggressively, because most ransomware is stopped by containment rather than recovery.
  • Decide the response criteria in advance, when nobody is panicking, and rehearse it.
